title: Not so Basic Instinct: Learning, Evolution, and the Behavioural Hypercycle
content: Traditional accounts of cognitive evolution often treat learning and instinct as zero-sum substitutes, in which increased behavioural plasticity necessarily displaces hard-wired routines. We challenge this view using a formal model of behavioural hypercycles: functionally integrated assemblies of behavioural components whose joint performance contributes to adaptive outcomes and promotes the persistence of the behavioural system itself. The model predicts that genetic assimilation proceeds selectively rather than uniformly. Rather than assimilating entire behaviours at once, evolution acts more like a greedy algorithm, preferentially canalizing behavioural bottlenecks that are difficult, costly, or reliability-limiting. Extending the model to multiple tasks reveals that behavioural reuse amplifies this process, causing recurrent behavioural primitives to experience disproportionately strong selection for canalization. Assimilation pressure therefore accumulates across the behavioural repertoires in which a component participates, favouring the stabilization of widely reused behavioural building blocks. Finally, allowing learning investment to evolve shows that learning and instinct remain local substitutes within fixed behavioural repertoires, but can become globally complementary when learning expands opportunities for behavioural reuse across tasks. Learning thereby acts as an engine of discovery, exposing reusable behavioural components to selection, while genetic assimilation progressively stabilizes them. The framework generates a range of testable predictions and provides a novel account of how sophisticated learning capacities may promote, rather than displace, the evolution of instinct.
